This is part I of a two-part series on this case study. You can find part II [here](./02_data_analysis.html "Cyclistic Case Study Part II - Analysis").  
The final presentation of the findings can be downloaded as a [Powerpoint](./cyclistic.pptx "Presentation - Powerpoint") or [PDF](./cyclistic.pdf "Presentation - PDF").

# Introduction

This is a case study in Google's Data Analytics Professional Certificate. The goal is to help Cyclistic, a fictitious bike-share company based in Chicago, convert casuals to members. The term casual refers to a user without a membership that either pays for each individual ride or purchases a day pass. Members have annual contracts - I go into more detail in [Part II](./02_data_analysis.html "Cyclistic Case Study Part II - Analysis"). We have been tasked to identify differences between the two using [historical trip data](https://divvybikes.com/system-data "Original data sets"), which has been provided by [Divvy](https://divvybikes.com/ "Divvy's website"). I wrote a [separate R script](./r_scripts/load.R) to import the data. The aim of this Markdown is to process it to prepare it for analysis.

# The data

First, we need to load the data and some packages that I'll be using a lot. I'll also source some functions for customized plots and tables.


```r
# Load packages
library("tidyverse")
library("kableExtra")

# Load data
load("data/r_data/data_raw.rda")
data <- data_raw

# Source functions
source("r_scripts/functions.R")
```

We can use dplyr's `glimpse()` to understand the data set's structure.

The data set is a record of 5.723.532 bike trips along with information regarding their time, (start and end) location, bike type and customer type. The data types seem sensible at first glance. The only thing I would like to change is replacing the inefficient character `ride_id` column with numeric IDs. In order to do so, we first need to make sure that all current ride IDs are unique.


```r
# Number of duplicate ride_ids
sum(duplicated(data$ride_id))
```

```
## [1] 0
```

There are no duplicates, so we can simply replace the IDs with consecutive integers without loosing any information.


```r
# Replace ride_id with integers
data <- data %>%
  mutate(ride_id = 1:n())
```

Also, ride duration might be interesting and can be easily computed.


```r
# Compute ride duration
data <- data %>%
  mutate(ride_duration = as.numeric(difftime(ended_at,
                                             started_at,
                                             units = "min")))
```

Here is what I see:

* `Rideable_type` and `member_casual` seem fine. They are both categorical with three/two categories and all their values fit into one of the categories. The distinction between classic, docked and electric bikes is a little strange, so we might want to investigate that later.
* All the values in `started_at` and `ended_at` have been classified as date-time. Values fall between April 1, 2021 and March 31, 2022 for started_at, which is in line with what we expected. Values for ended_at reach into April 1, 2022, so our data set apparently contains all the trips that started within April 2021 and March 2022, regardless of when they ended.
* Station names and IDs contain a lot of missing values. These values could be valid though, since bikes might not necessarily need to be parked at stations. However, `start_station_id` contains fewer missing values than `start_station_name`. We might be able to infer the missing names based on IDs, but perhaps the missing names indicate that something is wrong with these observations. We'll have to look into that.
* `Start_lat` and `start_lng` do not contain missing values, but their maximum values are suspicious, since they deviate a lot from the rest of the variables' summary statistics.
* `End_lat` and `end_lng` summary statistics are more sensible. However, these do contatin quite a few missing values. While missing start and end stations make sense, missing positions do not. Maybe these are indicators of technical errors, such as empty batteries, which would likely make the rest of the variables for these observations invalid as well.
* Values for `ride_duration` fall into a huge range of multiple weeks, even though the majority of values seem to fall into a much smaller range. Negative trip durations are impossible and trip durations of multiple days, while possible, do not make a lot of sense either and should be further investigated.

We can now dig deeper based on these preliminary findings. Particularly, we need to examine ride duration and all variables related to start and end locations. Let's start by looking at `ride_duration`.

# Ride duration I

## Distribution

After looking at some basic descriptive statistics earlier, I am interested in the distribution of ride durations.


```r
# Plot ride duration
data %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = ride_duration/60/24),
                 binwidth = 1, boundary = 0, color = "black") +
  xlab("ride_duration (days)")
```

![](01_data_processing_files/figure-html/histogram_01-1.png)<!-- -->

Since so many values fall between 0 and 24 hours, it is impossible to distinguish between other bins. Zooming in might help us understand these less common durations.


```r
# Plot ride duration zoomed in
data %>%
  my_ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = ride_duration/60/24),
                 binwidth = 1, boundary = 0, color = "black") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1000)) +
  xlab("ride_duration (days)")
```

![](01_data_processing_files/figure-html/histogram_zoom_01-1.png)<!-- -->

There are more than 625 trips with negative durations. Since start and/or end times of these observations are incorrect, their other measures might be wrong too and hence should not be included in the analysis. Before removing any observations though, I am interested whether ride durations differ between certain bike or membership types, so I'll create a table of summary statistics by group...


```r
# ride_duration extreme values by group
data %>%
  group_by(member_casual, rideable_type) %>%
  summarize(min = min(ride_duration),
            max = max(ride_duration),
            mean = mean(ride_duration),
            sd = sd(ride_duration),
            n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(percentage = n*100 / sum(n)) %>%
  kable_custom()
```

Key observations are:

* Negative trip durations occur in all groups and are only slightly more common (relatively) in electric bikes.
* Docked bikes seem to be responsible for all trips with a duration of more than 26 hours.
* Docked bikes stand out due to their high number of long trips and their relatively low number of total trips.

Unfortunately, I cannot find anything on docked bikes in either the case study scenario provided by Google (where there is no mention of electric bikes either), or Divvy's website (https://divvybikes.com/), who provide the real-world data set for this case study. Given that docked bikes stand out in terms of trip durations and the fact that they have only been used by casuals and I cannot find any explanations for either, I decided to remove these data points and continue my analysis without docked bikes. If this were a real-life case, I would obviously get help from others, however, I think looking at electric bikes vs classic bikes is sufficient for this case study.

## Removing outliers

I am going to track any changes I make along with their type (modification vs removal of observations) and their specific reasons in a changelog. In order to do so efficiently, I'll create a function that I'll be able to use whenever I modify or remove observations.


```r
# Custom function for tracking changes
track_changes <- function (data, data_old, changelog, type, reason) {
  # Extract affected rows
  cl_temp <- anti_join(data_old, data) %>%
    select(ride_id, member_casual, rideable_type) %>%
    add_column(type = type, reason = reason) %>% # add type and reason
    distinct() # select only distinct observations for long format
  
  # Bind to existing entries
  bind_rows(changelog, cl_temp)
}

# Set up changelog
changelog <- tibble()
```

Now that we're set up, we can delete the unneeded rows...


```r
# Copy of unchanged dataframe
data_old <- data

# Delete observations where rideable_type == docked_bike
data <- data %>% filter(rideable_type != "docked_bike")

# Remove unneeded factor level
data$rideable_type <- fct_drop(data$rideable_type)
```

... and record the changes we made.


```r
# Changelog entry
changelog <- track_changes(data, data_old, changelog, "removal", "docked_bikes")
```

I also found on [Divvy's website](https://divvybikes.com/system-data "Divvy data") that their data sets are not supposed to include any trips with a duration of less than 1 minute, since these are commonly caused by false starts or users trying to redock their bikes. Accordingly, I decided to remove these trips. This also takes care of trips with negative durations. Even though this might remove a small number of valid observations, the majority of the data points affected were most likely created through technical errors or other odd events and are thus invalid.


```r
# Copy of unchanged dataframe
data_old <- data

# Delete observations where ride_duration < 1 min
data <- data %>% filter(ride_duration >= 1)

# Changelog entry
changelog <- track_changes(data, data_old, changelog, "removal", "duration_<_1min")
```

## New distribution

Let's plot ride duration again for the remaining observations.


```r
# Plot ride duration again
data %>%
  my_ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = ride_duration/60),
                 binwidth = 1, boundary = 0, color = "black") +
  xlab("ride_duration (hours)")
```

![](01_data_processing_files/figure-html/histogram_02-1.png)<!-- -->

And zoomed in.


```r
# Plot ride duration again zoomed in
data %>%
  my_ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = ride_duration/60),
                 binwidth = 1, boundary = 0, color = "black") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 150000)) +
  xlab("ride_duration (hours)")
```

![](01_data_processing_files/figure-html/histogram_zoom_02-1.png)<!-- -->

This looks much better already. The range has gotten a lot smaller. However, there are still some very long trips and the spike in trips that took between 24 and 25 hours is particularly odd.

We could simply choose an arbitrary cutoff e.g. based on Tukey (upper quartile + 1.5*IQR), even though that one in particular seems a bit conservative in this case as it would throw out all trips with a duration of more than half an hour. Using the 99th percentile for example would leave us with only trips lasting less than 1 3/4 hours. An arbitrary cut off at 3 hours would leave us with 99.68% of observations.

Even though any arbitrary cutoff will almost certainly remove not only invalid observations, but valid ones as well, this could easily be justified by the fact that these extreme customer behaviors should not affect our marketing recommendations anyway. Instead, we should focus on properly targetting the majority of casuals, particularly the ones likely to convert (which are probably not the ones showcasing these extreme behaviors), rather than attempting to appeal to every single individual. However, I am curious whether there is a better way to filter out invalid observations using other variables that might be related to long trip durations. Accordingly, I will leave the data set as is for now.

# Start and end location

Other than trip duration, we also need to validate start and end stations and coordinates. Since there are certain relationships between station ID (`station_id`), name (`station_name`) and geographical coordinates (`lat` and `lng`), it makes sense to investigate them together rather than individually.

## Multiple missing values

First, lets look at missing values, beginning with observations in which both `start_station_id` and `start_station_name` are missing.


```r
# Missing start_station_name and start_station_id by rideable_type
data %>%
  select(start_station_name, start_station_id, rideable_type) %>%
  mutate(across(c(start_station_name, start_station_id), is.na)) %>%
  mutate(both = start_station_name & start_station_id) %>%
  group_by(rideable_type) %>%
  summarize(missing_values = sum(both)) %>%
  kable_custom()
```

Even though classic bikes are supposed to be parked at stations, that's obviously not always the case. Earlier, we also noticed that there were some missing geographic coordinates for end locations. Let's summarize these data points to see whether there is a connection.


```r

data %>%
  filter(is.na(end_lat) & is.na(end_lng)) %>%
  summary()
```

None of the observations with missing `end_lat` and `end_lng` have data for station name or ID that could be used to infer the missing values. Also notice that these are all classic bikes, more than three quarters of these trips were made by casuals and the ride durations are extremely high. Whether they represent cases of misuse or technical errors, these observations are very likely invalid and at the very least irrelevant for what we are looking to achieve. They can thus be removed.


```r
# Copy of unchanged dataframe
data_old <- data

# Remove where end_lat and end_lng are NA
data <- data %>% filter(!is.na(end_lat) | !is.na(end_lng))

# Changelog entry
changelog <- track_changes(data, data_old, changelog,
                           "removal", "no_geographical_coordinates")
```

Deleting these observations did not get rid of all missing values for `end_station_id` and `end_station_name` for classic bikes. However, the remaining observations at least have geographical coordinates that could be used to infer station names and IDs. Let's look at the summary statistics of those observations.


```r
data %>%
  filter((is.na(end_station_id) & rideable_type == "classic_bike")) %>%
  summary()
```

Apparently, these values are not missing at random, as their ride durations are highly different from the rest of the observations. I cannot see any reasons why this would be the case if these data points were valid, so I am going to delete them.


```r
# Copy of unchanged dataframe
data_old <- data

# Delete classic bike trip with no end station
data <- data %>%
  filter(!(is.na(end_station_id) & rideable_type == "classic_bike"))

# Changelog entry
changelog <- track_changes(data, data_old, changelog,
                           "removal", "classic_and_no_end_station")
```

## Missing station name or ID

Let's now look at observations where either station name **or** ID, and/or either latitude **or** longitude are missing. In order to do so efficiently for start and end locations at the same time, I am going to first reshape the data frame to a longer format, where start and end location of a given trip each make up distinct observations.


```r
# Long format for stations
data <- data %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = matches("^start_|^end_"),
               names_to = c("type", ".value"),
               names_pattern = '(^[^_]+(?=_))_(.*)') %>%
  mutate(type = as.factor(type))

# Glimpse
glimpse(data)
```

This format will make the upcoming operations much easier. Now we can look for observations with either missing station name **or** ID for start and end stations at the same time.


```r
# Find observations where one is missing
data %>%
  filter((is.na(station_name) & !is.na(station_id)) |
                       (is.na(station_id) & !is.na(station_name)) |
                       (is.na(lat) & !is.na(lng)) |
                       (is.na(lng) & !is.na(lat))) %>%
  kable_custom()
```

Each of the three IDs is associated with one specific station name, which is only missing for one observation. Since there is nothing curious about the observations, other than the missing station name, I will simply assign the station names based on their IDs. Now that the data is in this longer format, we need to be careful with our changelog, since two removed rows do not necessarily equate to two removed observations, since both rows could belong to the same trip. I am going to use "n" to refer to the number of deleted rows and "trips" to refer to the number of deleted observations.


```r
# Copy of unchanged dataframe
data_old <- data

# Assign station names based on station IDs
data <- data %>%
  mutate(station_name = as.factor(case_when(
    station_id == "13221" ~ "Wood St & Milwaukee Ave",
    station_id == "20215" ~ "Hegewisch Metra Station",
    station_id == "WL-008" ~ "Clinton St & Roosevelt Rd",
    TRUE ~ as.character(station_name))))

# Changelog entry
changelog <- track_changes(data, data_old, changelog,
                           "modification", "fix_NA_station_names")
```

## Station names associated with multiple IDs

Next, I would like to know whether there are any station names that are associated with more than one station ID.


```r
# Find station_names that are associated with multiple station_ids
data %>%
  mutate(start = ifelse(type == "start", TRUE, FALSE),
         end = ifelse(type == "end", TRUE, FALSE)) %>%
  group_by(station_name, station_id) %>%
  summarize(n = n(),
            start = as.logical(sum(start)),
            end = as.logical(sum(end))) %>%
  group_by(station_name) %>%
  filter(n() > 1) %>%
  kable_custom()
```

There are two station names in our data set that each are associated with two different IDs. We should try to find out whether, despite having two IDs, these station names still always refer to the same station. In order to do so, we can look at their geographical coordinates and the time frames in which each station has been used. We will only consider classic bike trips, since geographical coordinates are more variable for electric bikes and can vary even for individual stations.


```r
# Look at stations that are associated with multiple IDs
data %>%
  filter(station_name %in% c("Lakefront Trail & Bryn Mawr Ave",
                             "Loomis St & 89th St") &
           rideable_type == "classic_bike") %>%
  group_by(station_name, station_id, lat, lng) %>%
  summarize(min = min(started_at),
            max = max(started_at)) %>%
  kable_custom()
```

It seems that both stations were closed for a bit and then reopened under the same name but using a different ID. However, *Loomis St & 89th St* stayed in exactly the same location, while *Lakefront Trail & Bryn Mawr Ave* seemed to only have moved slightly. We can calculate the distance in meters via the Haversine Distance.


```r
# Distance between two station versions
geosphere::distHaversine(c(41.98404, -87.65231), c(41.98404, -87.65228))
```

```
## [1] 3.339585
```

Since *Loomis St & 89th St* has not moved at all and *Lakefront Trail & Bryn Mawr Ave* moved less than 3.5m, I think it makes sense for our purposes to treat both "versions" of each station as the same station. Hence, I will replace the old IDs with the new ones. But first, we need to make sure that neither of the IDs is associated with another station name.


```r
# Find all station names associated with IDs
data %>%
  filter(station_id %in% c("KA1504000152", "15576", "201022", "20102")) %>%
  group_by(station_id, station_name) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  kable_custom()
```

Seems like we're good to go, so we can simply replace the old IDs with the new ones.


```r
# Copy of unchanged dataframe
data_old <- data

# Same IDs for same stations
data <- data %>%
  mutate(station_id = as.factor(case_when(
    station_id == "KA1504000152" ~ "15576",
    station_id == "201022" ~ "20102",
    TRUE ~ as.character(station_id))))

# Changelog entry
changelog <- track_changes(data, data_old, changelog,
                           "modification", "multiple_IDs_for_same_station")
```

## Station IDs associated with multiple names

Now that we've looked at station names that are associated with multiple IDs, we can do the same the other way around.


```r
# Find station_IDs that are associated with multiple station_names
data %>%
  mutate(start = ifelse(type == "start", TRUE, FALSE),
         end = ifelse(type == "end", TRUE, FALSE)) %>%
  group_by(station_name, station_id) %>%
  summarize(n = n(),
            min = min(ride_duration),
            mean = mean(ride_duration),
            median = median(ride_duration),
            max = max(ride_duration),
            casuals_perc = 100*sum(member_casual == "casual")/n(),
            start = as.logical(sum(start)),
            end = as.logical(sum(end))) %>%
  group_by(station_id) %>%
  filter(n() > 1) %>%
  arrange(station_id) %>%
  relocate(2) %>%
  kable_custom() %>%
  scroll_box(width = "100%", height = "300px")
```

Since, by design, IDs can be associated with multiple names, it is not surprising that we found a few of those cases. I won't change those station names to be consistent, since it's perfectly possible that the names actually changed at some point. However, it is important to take this into account later when analyzing members and casuals regarding their station usage, when we might be better off using IDs rather than names. Other than that, the one thing that seems a bit strange is station "351" whose name is the same as its ID. However, other than what is apparently a naming error that only occurred twice, the station seems perfectly normal. I think we can simply change the station name for those two observations and keep them in our data set.


```r
# Copy of unchanged dataframe
data_old <- data

# Change station name according to ID
data <- data %>%
  mutate(station_name = ifelse(station_name == "351",
                        "Mulligan Ave & Wellington Ave",
                        as.character(station_name)) %>%
           as.factor())

# Changelog entry
changelog <- track_changes(data, data_old, changelog,
                           "modification", "ID_instead_of_name")
```

Based on their names, their very low traffic and the mostly unusual ride durations, these stations seem to be service or repair stations. They are probably used mainly for service trips and thus irrelevant to our analysis and can be removed.


```r
# Copy of unchanged dataframe
data_old <- data

# Delete observations where station ID and name are identical
data <- data %>%
  filter(as.character(station_id) != as.character(station_name) |
           is.na(station_id) | is.na(station_name))

# Changelog entry
changelog <- track_changes(data, data_old, changelog,
                           "removal", "identical_ID_and_name")
```

Now we should check if there are any other stations that contain the key words "test", "repair" or "charging".
 

```r
# Search for other stations
data %>%
  filter(if_any(matches("name$|id$"),
                ~ str_detect(.,regex("test|repair|charging",
                                     ignore_case = TRUE)))) %>%
  group_by(station_id, station_name) %>%
  summarize(n = n(),
            min = min(ride_duration),
            mean = mean(ride_duration),
            median = median(ride_duration),
            max = max(ride_duration),
            casuals_perc = 100*sum(member_casual == "casual")/n()) %>%
```

# Ride duration II

## Recheck distribution

All that's left to do now is examine ride duration in combination with start and end locations in order to possibly identify more invalid data points. First, we need to get the data frame back into its original format.


```r
# Keep only full observations (start and end)
duplicate_ids <- table(data$ride_id) %>% .[.>1] %>% names() %>% as.numeric()
data <- data %>% filter(ride_id %in% duplicate_ids)

# Transform long to wide
data <- data %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = "type",
              values_from = c("station_name", "station_id", "lat", "lng"),
              names_glue = "{type}_{.value}") %>%
  relocate(colnames(data_raw))

# Drop unneeded levels
data <- droplevels(data)
```

Plot trip duration again to see whether anything has changed.


```r
# Plot ride duration again
data %>%
  my_ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = ride_duration/60),
                 binwidth = 1, boundary = 0, color = "black") +
  xlab("ride_duration (hours)")
```

## Choosing a cut-off value

With the size of the current data set, a few invalid data points would probably not affect our analysis too much. Yet, for reasons mentioned earlier (properly focusing on the majority of customers and potential members rather than trying to please every single one and letting extreme customer behaviors affect our marketing, possibly resulting in not properly targeting any customers), I would like to exclude some more outliers. Since there is no clear cut-off or other criteria by which we can define outliers or identify invalid data points, we will simply have to make an arbitrary, albeit informed, decision.

According to their [website](https://divvybikes.com/pricing "Divvy pricing"), Divvy memberships include unlimited 45 minute rides, after which members need to either switch bikes or pay \$0.16 per minute. Non-members have to pay \$1 to unlock the bike and then start paying \$0.16 per minute straight from the start. A day pass includes unlimited 3-hour rides. Based on this information, it is relatively unlikely for anyone, member or casual, to ride their bike for more than three hours, since they could just switch bikes earlier to avoid any additional costs. Also, it would be pointless for customers that regularly do trips lasting 2 1/3 hours or longer to switch to a membership, because at \$0.16 per minute, a trip like that would already be more expensive than a day pass, even for a member that only starts paying after 45 minutes. Accordingly, unless Cyclistic are looking to change their membership conditions or pricing, these customers are not our targets for memberships. Yet, I will include every trip up to a duration of 4 hours. This will include people using a day pass and allows for a little margin on top of those three hours to include even those that perhaps miscalculated the duration of their trip or underestimated how long it would take them to get to the next station. However, I might subset the data set based on trip duration later in my analysis, depending on which question I am looking to answer.


```r
# Copy of unchanged dataframe
data_old <- data

# Exclude trip durations of more than 4 hours
data <- data %>% filter(ride_duration <= 240)

# Changelog entry
changelog <- track_changes(data, data_old, changelog,
                           "removal", "duration_>_240min")
```

# Wrap-up

## Add variables

Before summarizing the data again, let's add some time related variables that will be interesting to analyze later.


```r
# Add day of the week, weekend, weekm month, time of day and date
data <- data %>%
  mutate(day_of_week = lubridate::wday(started_at, label = T, week_start = 1),
         weekend = as.factor(ifelse(day_of_week %in% c("Sat", "Sun"),
                                    "weekend",
                                    "weekday")),
         week = lubridate::isoweek(started_at),
         month = lubridate::month(started_at, label = T, abbr = T),
         hour = lubridate::hour(started_at),
         minute = hour + lubridate::minute(started_at)/60,
         second = minute + lubridate::second(started_at)/3600,
         date = lubridate::date(started_at))
```

```r
  scroll_box(height = "300px", width = "500px")
```

## Save

Finally, we need to save the clean data, so that we can use it in our analysis. We'll also save the changelog to document and possibly communicate the cleaning process.


```r
# Save clean data
save(data, file = "data/r_data/data_cleaned.rda")

# Save changelog
save(changelog, file = "data/r_data/changelog.rda")
```
